issues.legal_issue: A will that directs a widow to adopt a son and directs the estate to be managed for that son may disclose an intention to benefit him with the estate even without an express devise.
material_facts: The testator authorized his widow to adopt a son and directed that, after adoption, the estate be held by the Court of Wards on the adopted son’s behalf.
The will contained no express devise of the estate to the son to be adopted.
issues.conclusion: The will impliedly intended the adopted son to take an estate of inheritance.
issues.legal_principle: A will is construed as a whole to ascertain the testator’s intention. The direction that the estate be managed on behalf of the adopted son after adoption implied that he was intended to be its beneficiary.

predicates.estate_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to property following the holder’s death.
predicates.will_authorizes_widow_to_adopt: The testator’s will authorizes the widow to adopt a son.
predicates.estate_directed_to_be_managed_for_adopte: The will directs that the estate be managed on behalf of the son after the widow adopts him.

issues.definition: When an estate succession dispute involves a will authorizing a widow to adopt and directing management for the adopted son, the son is treated as intended to benefit from the estate.

issues.legal_issue: A testamentary disposition made within the restricted period before the testator’s death is not barred when its beneficiary is a person who would have succeeded to the estate or an interest in it.
material_facts: The will was executed and attested less than three months before the testator died.
The will intended the son to be adopted by the widow to take the estate.
Under the statutory succession scheme, a son adopted by the widow with the testator’s authority would take the estate after the widow’s death.
issues.conclusion: The short interval between execution of the will and the testator’s death did not bar the adopted son from acquiring an interest under the will.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1) of the Oudh Estates Act 1869 restricted gifts and bequests to persons who would not have succeeded to the estate or an interest in it. An adopted son authorized by the testator was a person who would succeed under the Act. The Court relied on Maharani Indar Kunwar v. Maharani Jaipal Kunwar, L.R. 15 I.A. 127; Bhaiya Rabidat Singh v. Maharani Indar Kunwar, L.R. 16 I.A. 53; and Abdul Latif v. Abadi Begam, L.R. 61 I.A. 322.

predicates.estate_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns succession to an estate governed by a special statutory succession scheme.
predicates.testamentary_disposition_made_within_res: The testator executed and attested the will less than three months before death.
predicates.beneficiary_would_succeed_under_successi: The intended beneficiary would have succeeded to the estate or an interest in it under the applicable succession scheme.

issues.definition: A short interval before death does not bar a testamentary disposition in an estate succession dispute if the beneficiary would have succeeded under the applicable succession scheme.

issues.legal_issue: A widow who takes a statutory life estate on intestacy is not divested by a later adoption, and the adopted son has no transferable interest in the estate during her lifetime.
material_facts: The will’s intended devise to the son could become effective only after the widow adopted him, leaving the estate undisposed of by the will between the testator’s death and the adoption.
No person entitled under the earlier statutory succession categories succeeded before the widow, who took the estate for her lifetime.
The widow adopted the son under her husband’s authority, and the son executed a trust deed over the estate while she was still alive.
issues.conclusion: The widow’s interest was vested for her lifetime and was not defeated by the adoption; the adopted son had no interest in the estate during her lifetime and could not settle it by the trust deed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 22(7) and 22(8) of the Oudh Estates Act 1869 give the widow a life estate when the earlier statutory successors are absent, with the husband-authorized adopted son succeeding on her death. The Act is self-contained on the matters it regulates: Pandit Chandra Kishore Tewari v. Deputy Commissioner of Lucknow, L.R. 76 I.A. 17. The statutory succession scheme does not adopt the Hindu-law doctrine that an adoption relates back to the adoptive father’s death. The Court also relied on Babu Abdul Karim Khan v. Babu Hari Singh, 1 O.D. 264; Bisheshwar Baksh Singh v. Jang Bahadur Singh, A.I.R. 1930 Oudh 225; and Harnath Kuar v. Indar Bahadur Singh, L.R. 50 I.A. 69.

rule.if: special_estate_succession_dispute and no_prior_statutory_successor and widow_takes_estate_for_life and adoption_occurs_during_widows_lifetime and adopted_son_transfers_estate_during_widows_lifetime

predicates.special_estate_succession_dispute: The proceeding concerns succession to an estate governed by a statutory scheme that specifies the widow’s and adopted son’s succession rights.
predicates.no_prior_statutory_successor: No person in the succession categories preceding the widow is entitled to take the estate.
predicates.widow_takes_estate_for_life: The widow takes the estate for her lifetime after the earlier statutory successors are absent.
predicates.adoption_occurs_during_widows_lifetime: The widow adopts a son under the deceased holder’s authority while she is alive.
predicates.adopted_son_transfers_estate_during_wido: The adopted son purports to transfer or settle the estate before the widow dies.

issues.definition: Where the statutory succession scheme gives the widow a life estate and the adopted son transfers the estate while she is alive, the transfer is inoperative during her lifetime.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a widow’s title was extinguished by adverse possession cannot be raised for the first time on appeal when it was not pleaded or tried, and possession without effective exclusion does not establish adverse possession.
material_facts: The claim that the widow’s title had been extinguished by adverse possession was not raised at trial and was not included in the pleadings.
The estate was managed by the Court of Wards and later by the adopted son, but the widow lived with him and the evidence did not show that she was excluded from the estate or any part of it.
The widow received maintenance rather than managing the estate herself.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court properly refused to entertain the newly raised adverse-possession claim, and the circumstances described did not show effective deprivation of the widow’s possession sufficient to extinguish her title.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession presents mixed questions of law and fact and is effectively decided after the relevant facts are proved. Mere erroneous admission of another person’s title, without effective deprivation of possession, does not extinguish title by adverse possession.

predicates.civil_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning competing claims to property.
predicates.adverse_possession_claim_not_pleaded_or_: The party asserting adverse possession did not plead or litigate that claim at trial.
predicates.widow_not_effectively_excluded_from_prop: The widow was not effectively deprived of possession of the estate or any part of it.
predicates.possession_based_only_on_admission_of_an: The other person’s possession was accompanied only by an erroneous admission of that person’s title, without effective deprivation of the widow’s possession.

issues.definition: In a civil property appeal, a late adverse-possession claim does not extinguish the widow’s title when it was not pleaded or tried and her possession was not effectively excluded.

issues.legal_issue: The doctrine that feeds an after-acquired interest into an earlier transfer applies only when the transfer was made for consideration.
material_facts: The transferor executed a trust deed over an estate in which he had no present interest during the widow’s lifetime.
The transferor later acquired an interest in the estate after the widow’s death.
The trustees undertook administrative duties, but the trust deed did not satisfy the transferor’s debts and the transfer was not made for consideration.
issues.conclusion: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply to the trust deed because it was not a transfer for consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43 of the Transfer of Property Act applies where a person erroneously or fraudulently represents authority to transfer property and professes to transfer it for consideration. Undertaking duties under a trust deed, without consideration moving to the transferor, does not satisfy that requirement.

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns the validity or effect of a transfer of property.
predicates.transferor_later_acquires_interest: The transferor obtains an interest in the property after purporting to transfer it.
predicates.transfer_made_without_consideration: The transfer was not made in return for consideration moving to the transferor.

issues.definition: When a transferor later acquires an interest in property but made the earlier transfer without consideration, that later interest is not fed into the transfer.
